titleEn: God is our refuge and strength
progression: | Dm Dm | Bb C | Dm Dm | Gm A7 |
intro: Twelve verses in three stanzas, each closed by Selah, and the singers named in the first line are the sons of Korah rather than David. Two of the stanzas end with the same refrain, verses 8 and 12 word for word, which is how you can hear that this was written for a group with an answering part. The word to watch is the root m-w-t, to totter. Mountains totter into the sea in verse 3, kingdoms totter in verse 7, and in verse 6 the city does not. One verb, used three times, carries the whole argument.

stichs.en: For the leader; of the sons of Korah.
Upon alamot. A song.

verses.summary: Not a prayer but a filing note for the choirmaster. Alamot is a musical direction whose sense is lost, and the family credited is Korah's, not David's.

stichs.en: God is for us a refuge and strength,
a help in troubles, very much to be found.

verses.summary: Three nouns before a single verb: refuge, strength, help. The last word attaches to the verb, not to the nouns, so the claim is about availability rather than size.

stichs.en: Therefore we will not fear,
when the earth changes,
when mountains slip into the heart of the seas.

verses.summary: The conclusion is stated before the catastrophe that would test it. What is listed is not an army but the ground itself failing, the one emergency a fortress is no use against.

stichs.en: Let its waters roar and foam,
let mountains shake at its surging. Selah.

verses.summary: The sea behaves here the way it behaves everywhere in this book, as a hostile force with a will. Selah closes the first stanza with the world still moving.

stichs.en: A river, its channels gladden the city of God,
the holiest of the dwellings of the Most High.

verses.summary: Against the roaring sea, quiet water that has been divided into channels. Jerusalem has no river, so the picture is not a map of anything.

stichs.en: God is in her midst, she shall not totter;
God will help her at the turn of morning.

verses.summary: The verb of verse 3 returns, negated. Mountains slip, she does not. And the help lands at first light, which is the hour a besieged city expects the assault instead.

stichs.en: Nations roared, kingdoms tottered;
He gave forth His voice, the earth melts.

verses.summary: The roaring moves off the water and onto the nations, the same verb both times. Then one word from God undoes them, and the tense shifts to the present as it happens.

stichs.en: The LORD of hosts is with us;
the God of Jacob is a high tower for us. Selah.

verses.summary: The refrain. Two titles, one military and one ancestral, and each is given a position: alongside us, and above us at a height nothing reaches.

stichs.en: Come, look at the works of the LORD,
who has set desolations in the earth.

verses.summary: Two imperatives turn the psalm outward to whoever is listening. What we are sent to look at is not a rescue but a ruin, which is what the end of a war looks like from the surviving side.

stichs.en: He makes wars cease to the end of the earth;
He breaks the bow and snaps the spear,
He burns the carts in the fire.

verses.summary: The objects of the three verbs are equipment, not enemies. Peace here is not an agreement between kingdoms, it is the destruction of the means of fighting.

stichs.en: Let go, and know that I am God;
I will be exalted among the nations,
I will be exalted in the earth.

verses.summary: The only verse in the psalm spoken by God, and it begins with a command to release rather than a command to be quiet. The hands being addressed are still holding something.

stichs.en: The LORD of hosts is with us;
the God of Jacob is a high tower for us. Selah.

verses.summary: The refrain comes back with nothing revised, now that the voice from outside has spoken. The same sentence, with the testimony of verses 9 to 11 behind it.

pardes.body: Three stanzas, each shut with Selah at verses 4, 8 and 12. The first is the world coming apart: earth, mountains, sea. The second is a city that does not come apart, watered by a river with channels rather than by a sea. The third is history, nations and kingdoms, ending in the destruction of weapons. The refrain of verses 8 and 12 is the congregation's line, and the fact that it does not appear after verse 4 has led many readers to suppose it dropped out there; that is a proposal about the text, not something the manuscripts show. The last word before each Selah is a claim already made, and the psalm never argues for it. It only widens the frame until the claim has been said in three sizes.

The psalm is held together by two roots repeated across its stanzas, and both are visible in the transliteration. The root m-w-t, to totter or give way, runs through {{3.6}}, {{6.3}} and {{7.2}}: mountains give way, the city does not, kingdoms do. The root h-m-h, to make a loud noise, runs from {{4.0}}, the waters, to {{7.0}}, the nations, so the two halves of the psalm are describing the same disturbance twice. Two words in it are genuinely unsettled. {{1.4}}, the direction over the title, is read as a reference to young women and so to high voices, or as the name of a tune or an instrument, and the case for either is thin. {{3.4}} is a causative form of the root m-w-r, to exchange or alter, so the line says the earth swaps its nature rather than merely moves; some translations render it as the earth being removed, which needs a different root.

The singers in the superscription are the descendants of the man the ground opened to swallow (Numbers 16:32), and Numbers 26:11 goes out of its way to record that his sons did not die. A song about ground that gives way, credited to that family, is a strange coincidence to leave unnoticed, and it makes the refrain sound less like a slogan and more like something learned. Verse 10 is read across the tradition as a description of the world to come rather than of any past battle, alongside Isaiah 2:4, where the same weapons are not burned but reforged into farm tools. The two images differ on what happens to the metal, and that difference is the whole question of whether the end of war is a repair or a clearing away. Verse 11 is spoken by God to everyone at once, which is why it is usually quoted alone, out of the psalm.

In the kabbalistic reading the sea and the river are two ways the same water arrives: undivided and destructive, or divided into channels and life-giving, and {{5.0}} is the second of these, the flow that reaches a place small enough to receive it. The city with God in her midst is the standard image of indwelling presence, feminine in the Hebrew throughout verse 6, and the help that comes at {{6.7}}, the turning of the morning, is read as the point where night has finished rather than as sunrise. Verse 11 is then not addressed to enemies but to the reader: {{11.0}} is a verb of slackening the grip, and knowing follows from letting go, in that order and not the other.
